entities.name: Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti (died 1280) was a prominent Florentine nobleman, banker, and suspected Epicurean philosopher whose posthumous fame rests almost entirely on his vivid portrayal in Dante Alighieri's *Inferno*, Canto X. A key figure in the turbulent Guelph-Ghibelline political landscape of 13th-century Florence, he represented a sophisticated intellectual stratum within the city's ruling elite, even as his philosophical leanings placed him outside orthodox Christian thought. His historical importance is amplified by his paternity of Guido Cavalcanti, a celebrated poet and close friend of Dante, thereby connecting him directly to the nascent period of Italian vernacular literature and the intellectual ferment of the Duecento.

Born into the powerful Cavalcanti family, one of Florence's oldest and most influential aristocratic lineages, Cavalcante was deeply embedded in the city's commercial and political life. While specific details of his philosophical writings or direct teachings are scarce, contemporary accounts and later literary interpretations suggest a strong adherence to Epicureanism, a Hellenistic philosophy emphasizing atomic materialism and the pursuit of pleasure (often understood as tranquility). This intellectual position, which denied the immortality of the soul, was considered heretical by the medieval Church and led to his condemnation to the Sixth Circle of Hell in Dante's epic poem, alongside other Epicureans like Farinata degli Uberti, for 'having made the soul die with the body.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti's primary significance stems from his vivid portrayal in Dante's *Inferno*, which immortalized him as a literary symbol of Epicureanism and paternal grief, thereby shaping the cultural understanding of philosophical dissent in the late Medieval period. His connection to the Cavalcanti family and his son, Guido, also links him to the development of early Italian vernacular literature.
